notes.heading: Chemical Reaction
notes.text: A chemical reaction is a process in which one or more substances change into new substances with different properties. The substances that take part in a chemical reaction are called reactants, and the new substances formed are called products.
points: Reactants are the substances that take part in a chemical reaction.
Products are the new substances formed in a chemical reaction.
A chemical reaction may be identified by a change in colour, change in temperature, formation of a gas, formation of a precipitate, or change in physical state.
Example: Magnesium burns in oxygen to form magnesium oxide: \(\ce{Mg + O2 -> MgO}\).

notes.heading: Chemical Equation
notes.text: A chemical equation is a short symbolic representation of a chemical reaction using the symbols and chemical formulae of the substances involved.
points: A chemical equation tells us which substances react and which substances are formed.
Example: Hydrogen and oxygen form water: \(\ce{H2 + O2 -> H2O}\).
The substances on the left side of the arrow are reactants.
The substances on the right side of the arrow are products.
The arrow means 'forms' or 'gives'.
Chemical Reaction = Actual process.
Chemical Equation = Symbolic representation of the process.

notes.heading: 1.1 Chemical Equations
notes.text: A chemical equation is a symbolic representation of a chemical reaction. Instead of writing the names of substances, their chemical symbols and formulae are used.
points: Example: Hydrogen + Oxygen → Water.
Using chemical formulae: \(\ce{H2 + O2 -> H2O}\).
\(\ce{H2}\) and \(\ce{O2}\) are the reactants.
\(\ce{H2O}\) is the product.
The arrow means 'forms' or 'gives'.

notes.heading: 1.1.1 Writing a Chemical Equation
notes.text: A chemical equation represents a chemical reaction using the symbols and formulae of the substances involved.
points: Write the reactants on the left-hand side.
Write the products on the right-hand side.
Separate reactants and products using an arrow.
Example: Magnesium + Oxygen → Magnesium oxide.
Using chemical formulae: \(\ce{Mg + O2 -> MgO}\).
\(\ce{Mg}\) and \(\ce{O2}\) are reactants, while \(\ce{MgO}\) is the product.
A skeletal chemical equation represents the reaction but is not balanced.
General form: \(\ce{Reactants -> Products}\).

notes.heading: 1.1.2 Balanced Chemical Equations
notes.text: A balanced chemical equation is an equation in which the number of atoms of each element is equal on both sides of the equation. This is based on the Law of Conservation of Mass, which states that mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.
points: Example of an unbalanced equation: \(\ce{Mg + O2 -> MgO}\).
There are 2 oxygen atoms on the left but only 1 oxygen atom on the right.
The balanced equation is: \(\ce{2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO}\).
The number of atoms of every element must be equal on both sides.
While balancing an equation, change only the coefficients, not the chemical formulae.
Example: \(\ce{2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O}\).
Number of atoms on LHS = Number of atoms on RHS.
A balanced chemical equation obeys the law of conservation of mass.

notes.heading: 1.2 Types of Chemical Reactions
notes.text: Chemical reactions can be classified into different types depending on how the reactants change into products.
points: Combination reaction.
Decomposition reaction.
Displacement reaction.
Double displacement reaction.
Oxidation and reduction reactions.

notes.heading: 1.2.1 Combination Reaction
notes.text: A combination reaction is a reaction in which two or more substances combine to form a single product.
points: General form: \(\ce{A + B -> AB}\).
Two or more reactants combine to form only one product.
Calcium reacts with oxygen to form calcium oxide: \(\ce{2Ca + O2 -> 2CaO}\).
Hydrogen reacts with oxygen to form water: \(\ce{2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O}\).
Carbon combines with oxygen to form carbon dioxide: \(\ce{C + O2 -> CO2}\).
Easy identification: Two or more reactants → One product.

notes.heading: 1.2.2 Decomposition Reaction
notes.text: A decomposition reaction is a reaction in which one compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances. It is the opposite of a combination reaction.
points: General form: \(\ce{AB -> A + B}\).
One reactant breaks down to form two or more products.
On heating calcium carbonate: \(\ce{CaCO3 ->[heat] CaO + CO2}\).
Water can be decomposed by electricity: \(\ce{2H2O ->[electricity] 2H2 + O2}\).
Heat causes thermal decomposition.
Electricity causes electrolytic decomposition.
Light causes photolytic decomposition.
Easy identification: One reactant → Two or more products.

notes.heading: 1.2.3 Displacement Reaction
notes.text: A displacement reaction is a reaction in which a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound.
points: General form: \(\ce{A + BC -> AC + B}\).
Element A is more reactive than element B and therefore displaces B.
Zinc reacts with copper sulphate: \(\ce{Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu}\).
Zinc is more reactive than copper.
Iron displaces copper from copper sulphate: \(\ce{Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu}\).
Easy identification: More reactive element + Compound → New compound + Less reactive element.

notes.heading: 1.2.4 Double Displacement Reaction
notes.text: A double displacement reaction is a reaction in which two compounds exchange their ions to form two new compounds.
points: General form: \(\ce{AB + CD -> AD + CB}\).
The ions of the two compounds exchange places.
Sodium sulphate reacts with barium chloride: \(\ce{Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4 + 2NaCl}\).
\(\ce{BaSO4}\) is an insoluble white solid called a precipitate.
A double displacement reaction that forms a precipitate is also called a precipitation reaction.
Easy identification: Two compounds → Two new compounds.

notes.heading: Oxidation
notes.text: Oxidation can be understood as the addition of oxygen, removal of hydrogen, or loss of electrons.
points: Addition of oxygen is oxidation.
Removal of hydrogen is oxidation.
Loss of electrons is oxidation.
Example: \(\ce{2Cu + O2 -> 2CuO}\).
Copper combines with oxygen, so copper is oxidised.

notes.heading: Reduction
notes.text: Reduction can be understood as the removal of oxygen, addition of hydrogen, or gain of electrons.
points: Removal of oxygen is reduction.
Addition of hydrogen is reduction.
Gain of electrons is reduction.
Example: \(\ce{CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O}\).
Oxygen is removed from copper oxide, so copper oxide is reduced.

notes.heading: Oxidation and Reduction Together — Redox Reaction
notes.text: When oxidation and reduction occur in the same reaction, the reaction is called a redox reaction.
points: Example: \(\ce{CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O}\).
\(\ce{CuO}\) loses oxygen → Reduction.
\(\ce{H2}\) gains oxygen → Oxidation.
Oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously.
Oxidation + Reduction = Redox Reaction.

notes.heading: 1.3 Effects of Oxidation Reactions in Everyday Life
notes.text: Oxidation reactions also occur in everyday life. Two important effects of oxidation are corrosion and rancidity.
points: Corrosion can cause damage to metals.
Rancidity can affect food containing fats and oils.
The two important effects are corrosion and rancidity.

notes.heading: 1.3.1 Corrosion
notes.text: Corrosion is the process in which a metal is gradually destroyed or damaged due to reactions with substances present in the environment, such as oxygen, moisture and acids.
points: Rusting of iron is a common example of corrosion.
Iron reacts with oxygen and moisture to form rust.
Rust is mainly hydrated iron(III) oxide: \(\ce{Fe2O3.xH2O}\).
The reddish-brown coating seen on iron objects is rust.
Copper develops a green coating of basic copper carbonate.
Silver develops a black coating of silver sulphide.
Corrosion can be prevented by protecting the metal from contact with air and moisture.
Common methods include painting, oiling or greasing, galvanisation and alloying.
Corrosion = Gradual damage of a metal due to environmental reactions.

notes.heading: 1.3.2 Rancidity
notes.text: Rancidity is the process in which food containing fats and oils gets oxidised, causing an unpleasant smell and taste.
points: When oily food is exposed to air for a long time, it may develop a bad smell and taste.
This happens because fats and oils undergo oxidation.
Rancidity can be prevented or slowed down by adding antioxidants to food.
Keeping food in airtight containers reduces contact with oxygen.
Refrigeration slows down oxidation.
Some foods are packed using nitrogen gas instead of oxygen.
Chips packets are often filled with nitrogen gas to prevent the oils from coming into contact with oxygen.
Rancidity = Oxidation of fats and oils causing unpleasant smell and taste.
